blocks.x: I mentioned the date is August the 19th, 1961, and we're interviewing, your name is Clarence?
Clarence Joseph Gabriel.
Clarence Joseph Gabriel. Can you tell us your birth date?
My birth date was 1905.
1905. And can you tell us anything about your father and your other brothers, as much as you can remember about your family, some of the musicians that you played with early too?
That was when I quite started getting into music again, way back in 1925.
By the way, where were you born? Was it right in town here?
Yeah, 409 up near them.
Right here in New Orleans.
Right in town, where they call us.
Where did your family come from?

Well, my mother come from Mobile, Alabama, but I wasn't sure where my father was from. But he had explained to me that my grandmother had come from St. Dominguez. Oh, yes. But he never did give me that town of Eastwood. What instrument you played for you, is the bandit or the piano? No, he stomped me off on drums.
Is that your father?

My father. What did your father play? He played trumpet. Oh, he played trumpet. He had the national office. The national? National office. No, no. Y'all don't have no pictures of it around here? No. I don't believe they're taking any pictures of it in the mids, you know. I don't believe they're taking them. Can you tell us anything more about your father? Going back to your father for a little while, can you tell us, do you know where he learned to play the trumpet? Well, he did. He started around a place called Pretty Grouse. That was around at Oldenst, Corn Island and Liberty. And then they had a place around here called 25. Yeah, I remember that. During the 10th Kennedy, what he had showed us, because he had started off on accordion. That was his first leading instrument played, accordion. And one of the gentlemen, he called Kaiser, he told him, he said, man, you play so swell on that accordion. He said, why don't you switch to some blowing instrument? Kaiser the one who plays safe on the clarinet? No, not him. This is the white drum. Oh, yeah? Oh, yeah? Yeah.

Seems like I heard of a man by the name of Kaiser that had a place they called the pig ankle or something where they'd kick the ham and all that. That's right. That's right. Absolutely. Down there in the district, near the 25. That's correct. Run by Kaiser. That's correct.

And he had given me his first trumpet. He told him, he said, well, man, you get off that squeeze box. That's what they call it. They said, I'll be playing so much squeeze box. I don't know that trumpet. And he started taking lessons with the fellow. Asibiyah, they called him. What's his name? A French fellow called Asibiyah. Asibiyah. Asibiyah. Asibiyah. That's what he used for his teacher. So he started writing his trumpet. And after he started writing his trumpet, when he started leading the band, the trumpet. After that. Do you know any more about this French teacher, Asibiyah? No. No, I don't exactly know because I was so young when he was teaching me that. He started learning.
Did he say if he played dance music or if he played classical or opera or anything?

No, he played nothing but jazzical music. You understand? Through the can-can-finish. He used to play waltz or for a drill. You know all of them, they played that kind of music. Do you remember, was that a B-flat cornet or? It was. It was a B-flat trumpet. A trumpet? Not a trumpet. It was a real cornet. Real cornet. Yeah, short cornet. The trumpets didn't come out until later years. And that was a B-flat horn, B-flat cornet. They called them trumpets around about, when it was the way in the late years of the 20s. When it won, I think. Yeah, when they took up the trumpet. When he was still teaching you music, was he still playing? He was still playing. Do you remember where or with who he was playing? Well, he had his own orchestra, you see, and he used to play out there all around the lake. Like called Over the Ride. It was out there around the Spanish boat, Millenway. Then there's another place, this big restaurant here, out here in Bunktown. That's what I remember in the morse. He used to give dances too out at Bunktown. Bunktown is right at the foot of the seawall. That's Bunktown. Right where the seawall started. In the west end there, huh? Yeah, right where the seawall started. Right where the mile line club. That's the start of the seawall. Do you remember any of the musicians that were playing with your father that time? Well, that was called the old Gatsby. He used to play bass. No, it was the trombone player. Vic was that? Vic Gatsby. Vic Gatsby. And, well, I used to use my cousin, dude, he used to call me, Albert Gabriel. He was the clarinet player. Dude, dude. Albert Gabriel. He was the clarinet player. And, Jonathan Sear, he was the guitar player. And, basically, I was called the old man Alphonse Gatsby. Alphonse Gatsby. Alphonse Gatsby. Alphonse Gatsby. Was that any relates to Vic and the... Well, it's supposed to be cousins. See, we never did get that straight. Yeah. It was supposed to be just the cousins. Yeah, it was related. I was trying to tell you. Dude, that's the one I was trying to tell you. Was playing B-flat Landry and the Holy Ghost Band. I was playing E-flat Landry. Remember, I couldn't remember his name. I didn't remember him. But that's who was playing, because his father was playing trumpet too. And his father, Big Landry, Pinchback, Two Rows. That's the name I was trying to remember when I was talking to you. Did you say your father taught you? Well, yeah, he showed us how to... Man and two? Man and two. He took man on the drum. That's what made man switch off on the drum to the clarinet. Because he didn't like that token of the drum. Yeah, two halves of the car. Two halves of the car. So, he got off the drum and he was clarinet. I got the release place in the drum. It's at the drum.
Did you tell us your father's name, his first name? His first name is Martin. Martin.
Martin Manuel Gabriel.
How long has he been dead now, about? Do you know when he...

He died right around 32. He died 32. You say you first started on the drum. He was starting on the drums. How long did you study the drums with your father? Well, I didn't kick up and amuse it with the drums. You understand? I just taught the playing by air. Whatever, you know, my rhythm. You kept up with the drums. It wasn't nothing but by air like that. So, I switched off the drums myself and I got on danger.
How old were you when you started on drums?

I was about... I was about... I was about around... 15, 16, like that when I played with him. I was back around the 20, 21. And how long did you stay with the drums? Well, I stayed with him for a good while. Then I started picking up the banjo and started learning how to read the banjo. I hadn't been playing piano since I was about 10. Oh, you had? Oh, you started on the piano? You started the piano first. I started the piano first, but still I never could read too good with the piano. So, I picked up the banjo. That's what I learned the banjo from my piano. I picked the notes off the piano. I learned from the ABCs like that on my banjo. Oh, yeah. In other words, you've been playing the piano since you was 10. Since I was about 15, you went on drums. Yeah, I went on drums and came to play the banjo. How long did you start playing the banjo? Oh, I started back in 25 and I stood on banjo until about 34. You played some banjo? Good man. I stood on banjo until about 34. But then that's when I started playing these big bands. The first band I started to play, I used to travel around with Sam Morgan and them to play the other fellas plays all the time, called Johnny Deeb. Yeah, Johnny Deeb. And then I went over and started playing with Louis DeVene. That was the next band I started playing. Our first little band that we made up was from King Howard. And made up our whole little band in the other year. And another fella, I think it was George Lewis and Clarence and King Howard on trumpet. Rudolph, uh... Big Rock on drums. Yeah, he was on drums. I think, I think, before we, me with Sam, playing Trimble. And another fella, who was Steve, he was the one of the clarinet. Steve Angle was that band? Steve Angle. That's right. And who was this Sam on the Trimble? Sam, uh, what you could call him. That's Sam, uh, what you could call him. That's Sam, they want some fellowship, huh? No, he joined church, he could play music years ago. I'm trying to think of him. I used to know his name really good. I'm trying to think of his name. I'm trying to think of his name. I believe it was Sam Robinson, they used to call him. Because we had so many nicknames for probably some of us. Yeah, I know. We couldn't keep up with it. But I believe his real name was Sam Robinson. I know. Mm-hmm. I know. And, uh, and Manny, he was playing before you? He was. He was. He was. He was, uh, playing, uh, playing drumming in the band with my boys at that time. And he switched off on Clarelet.
Is he much older than you?

Manny was the old? Well, he is. He's about seven years old. Seven years old. All right. You played with Kidronale a while too, didn't you? Oh, I did. I played with Kidronale. I played with, uh, Kid Brother for a while. Oh, yeah. With his band. And, uh, oh, there were so many bands. Yeah. Probably the beginning of the street. Uh-huh.
I was going to ask some more about Louis Dumaine band. Did you make any records with Louis Dumaine when he made those? Well, I did. He made some for Victor once.

I didn't have a chance to make no records with the boys. But, uh, they had made records. And, uh, time the fellas, no fella come, I don't know if he come out of New York or way. But he had come from, from up to nine, you see. And, uh, a little fella called Leonard, he had played in my place, you see, made the records. But after that, I stood in the band with him. And we played, uh, I went to a dance hall.
We played from around about 25.

Around 26, I believe, from about around 27. So, all the doing that, that next year is when I went to a dance hall. We had so many engagements during them years, back in 27. We played our chair by Jack Sheen. We played on the boat, the captain. We played at the Junk Hotel. We played at the Rosecrunk Hotel. We played at the Rosecrunk Hotel. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. booth and have a restaurant. We had been playing for so many times, all during the music, so many different engagements that we played. I believe it's all right here on T'Nan and Ramport. I believe I played dance. You know all engagements and it's a part, but I went into the dance hall and I played there kind of regular. I played there with Ralph Foster. Car said there, leading the band, and I played with him. He's a band then. Ralph Foster's band. We left there, I left there, and we come around here and I played with Mike DeLay by the LaVita. I stood there until 34. What was the LaVita? Right next to the point on I was building. We had a dance hall. That's the place I was telling you me and Pai Joe played the last dance there. We closed it up. We was playing there when the place closed up for good. Did we get the location on the tape? That's on Iberville between Maganda and Ramport. You know right where that lot is, the parking lot? Right next to that parking lot because we used to go in through the parking lot to go in the back door. You know, get right to the bandstand. The bandstand was in the back of the hall? Yeah. Was it raised? Oh yeah, the bandstand was raised. How high? About like a stage. Four feet or something like that? Yeah, about four feet I would say. We had one in the middle of the front next door. See? And laying on, the chance of the Budweiser.
That was near Ramport Street then?

The Budweiser, no. The front was near Ramport. Close to the Ramport. Close to the Ramport. That was some rough days. The Budweiser went there. The Budweiser went there in 1930. We would come off to Dixie. The Budweiser was looking for us and he came. That's when we went to the Laveena. Mike stayed there. Mike stayed there a long time. He laid on Albert Fernandes playing piano with him. He'd swap up the trumpet to piano. See, Albert played piano and he played piano. He'd swap up and let the rest of the lip up. Then I laid on, but if it happened, that's when we gave it away. Who did you say was on those records playing banjo with Louis Demain? A little fella called Leonard. Leonard. I'm trying to give you the best name. You may think of it.

I was going to ask some more about some of the pieces that you played with Louis Demain. Did he write many numbers? I know when he made the records he had the number he called Franklin Street Blues and Red Onion Drag. I wonder, did you ever play those in the dance band that you worked with him?

Well, after we started playing, see like all these big clubs, the Sun Yacht Club, and all this country. They started playing nothing with stock. They wouldn't play them. They would normally like the rice. They played mostly stock. They had to build their dear

The 17th Street Canal Every night I'd get me a... Well they call it the 17th Street Canal where they say. Well the 17th Street Canal was run into it. Yeah, where it goes right into the lake. That's where it sits, right off the lake. Canal right there by the 17th Street Canal. That's Brooklyn. Right on the corner. I think that's the line for Jefferson Parish too. That's what I was trying to get together. Right on the line of Jefferson Parish.
That used to play out the Beerus too.
Hmm?
Used to play in the Beerus too. Oh yeah. Arnensboro, the Lothel Street.

Down the Beerus? Down the river. That is it. Right by Hatch. Boywoods. Used to play way down in the mountain. Boywood is that place where you have to get the boat to go. And the Beerus you have to take that mail boat and go. Mail boat and go down the river. That's Ireland. They got the rec resort, they got the grocery, they got the dance hall. They got the oil station. Most boats stopped and refueled. Call it Boywood. I used to play that with Paul Moje. Yeah, absolutely. Old man Moje, Lacroix. That's correct. Yeah, whenever they get Lacroix here, you know. Back to Bradley Street. Whenever you get him. Yeah, that's right. Yeah. Well, that was another little band that we had together. Lacroix, Fyre. Yeah. I never did know his name. Who? Fyre, Big Fyre, the Crabone Plant. Oh yeah. And this little barrister, but he died here. Yeah. He made up a little band and monks out with stuff. Little choir and all of them. Yeah. There was nothing on there. I forgot all about it. Made up during them. That's when I first started learning how to play. George McCombe. Yeah. Well, George. You see. Yeah. He. Lewis took six. And he played in these places. George McCombe played in Lewis Domains. In Lewis Domains. In Lewis Domains. Yeah, well George played in Lewis's place you see. Lewis took six. George McComb played in Lewis DeMaine's. In Lewis DeMaine's place. He took the band over to him and Oliver. Oliver was coming to band playing. Yeah, playing sax, he played trumpet. Oliver what? Alcon. Oliver Alcon. Alcon, that's right. C-L-C brothers. Alvin. Alvin. Alvin. Alvin's brother. Well, George McCombs, I think, was George McCombs's step-brothers. Oh, they were. That's right. Do you remember when we interviewed the Mrs. McCombs and so on? Yeah, I remember. Neil Pe bamboo

segments.title: Opening, birth date and return to music in 1925
segments.summary: Interviewer gives the date, August 19, 1961; Gabriel gives his name and 1905 birth, and says he got back into music around 1925.

segments.title: Birthplace in New Orleans and family origins
segments.summary: Born in New Orleans; mother from Mobile, grandmother from Santo Domingo; his father started him on drums.

segments.title: Father's switch from accordion to trumpet, Kaiser and teacher Asibiyah
segments.summary: His father began on accordion; Kaiser, who ran a place in the District, urged him to switch to a blowing instrument, gave him a trumpet, and a French teacher taught him.

segments.title: Father's orchestra, lakefront dances and band members
segments.summary: His father led an orchestra playing dances around the lake and Bucktown, with Vic Gaspard, cousin Albert Gabriel and others; his father is named as Martin Manuel Gabriel.

segments.title: Father's death and playing drums by ear
segments.summary: His father died around 1932; Gabriel played drums by ear and then switched off them.

segments.title: From drums and piano to banjo, early bands and brother Manny
segments.summary: He played piano from about 10, drums around 15 or 16, then learned banjo from 1925 to 1934, playing with Sam Morgan, Louis Dumaine and others; his older brother Manny moved from drums to clarinet.

segments.title: Louis Dumaine's band and the Victor records
segments.summary: Asked about Louis Dumaine's records, he says another banjoist, Leonard, played in his place on the Victor sides, and he stayed in the band afterwards.

segments.title: Engagements, Ralph Foster and Mike DeLay at the Lavida dance hall
segments.summary: Lists hotel and boat engagements around 1927, then playing with Ralph Foster and Mike DeLay at the Lavida on Iberville until 1934, describing the hall and its bandstand.

segments.title: Playing Dumaine's numbers versus stock arrangements at clubs
segments.summary: Asked whether the Dumaine tunes were played in dance work, he says the big clubs wanted stock arrangements; the rest is garbled ASR.

segments.title: Lakefront and river-parish playing spots, Lacroix's band and McCombs
segments.summary: Recalls playing near the 17th Street Canal, down the river at Boothville, with Lacroix and others, and how George McCombs took over Dumaine's band, with Oliver Alcorn.
